how-much-to-charge-for-home-staging.html.text:
HOME STAGING PRICING

You quote a term. You pay for a duration.

The search is usually “how much to charge for home staging.” Most of the answers are a rate card from a franchise with a warehouse team, or a lead form. This page is the method an independent stager can actually check against their own invoices, and it pairs with a free browser calculator that does the arithmetic locally — nothing you type leaves your device.

A staging job is two costs wearing one price

Install day and pickup day are fixed. Crew hours, the truck, the round trip, the equipment, the consultation: those cost the same whether the listing closes in three weeks or sits until spring. Then there is the part nobody quotes — the package itself is off the market for the whole term. Storage, insurance, and wear keep running, and that sofa cannot be delivered to a second listing while it is in the first one.

The trap is that the first cost is easy to see on an invoice and the second one is not. It shows up as a warehouse bill you would be paying anyway, so it gets treated as overhead rather than as a cost this specific job is consuming.

Build the included term first

Add the fixed cost: crew hours at a loaded rate, mileage at whatever you actually reimburse, equipment, the flat consultation fee, and anything else the job carries. Then add the furniture package’s own carrying cost, per month, multiplied by the term you are including. That total is your break-even for a job that finishes exactly on schedule. Overhead as a share of direct cost and a target margin as a share of price sit on top of it.

Note what this means: two jobs with identical room counts have different floors if one ties up your good package for two months and the other borrows a spare bedroom set for three weeks.

Then price the month you did not plan for

The extension fee is where independent stagers lose the margin they priced. It is easy to set it by feel — a round number that sounds reasonable to a nervous seller who has already dropped the asking price once. If that number is below what the package costs you to carry for a month, the fee is not compensation, it is a subscription you are paying to the listing.

The calculator states this as a straight comparison: profit per extension month, and how many extra months the job can absorb before the whole thing goes negative. When the fee clears the carrying cost, a slow listing is merely disappointing. When it does not, a slow listing is expensive, and it gets worse every month for a reason you cannot influence.

Reconcile after the home sells

Time on market is unknowable at quote time, so the estimate was always a planning number. Once the listing closes, put the real months back in and look at what the job actually earned. Do that a dozen times and you have something better than a rate card: your own distribution of how long your listings really take, in your market, at your price point. That is the figure that should set your included term.

What this is not

Not a quote on your behalf, not an industry rate card, not legal, tax, or business advice, and not a prediction of how long any home will take to sell. It models a vacant-listing furniture package; occupied-home staging consultations are priced differently. Verify every figure against your own invoices, storage bills, and mileage log before you send a price.

Open the home staging bid calculator — it stays in your browser.

Common questions

How much should I charge for home staging?

There is no single rate, because a staging job is not one price but two. The first is a fixed cost paid on delivery day and pickup day: crew hours, the truck, mileage, equipment, and the consultation. The second is a monthly cost that runs for as long as the furniture sits in the house: storage you are still paying for, insurance, and wear on a package that cannot be rented to anyone else. Price the included term to cover the fixed cost plus the carrying cost for that many months, then add overhead and your target margin.

How much should a home staging extension fee be per month?

At an absolute minimum, more than what one month of that furniture package actually costs you to keep off the market. Work out storage, insurance, and depreciation per month for the package itself, not for the whole warehouse, and treat that figure as the floor. An extension fee set below it turns every extra month on the market into a larger loss, and the loss has no ceiling because you do not control when the home sells.

Why does a staging job that sold slowly lose money?

Because the quote covered a term and the cost ran for a duration. Install and de-install cost the same whether the listing sells in three weeks or four months, so a term price that looks healthy on a fast sale is doing all its work in the first few weeks. Every month past the included term draws down the same margin unless the extension fee covers the carrying cost on its own. A job can be quoted at a thirty percent margin and finish near zero without a single number in the quote being wrong.

Should I price home staging per room?

A room count is useful for describing the job to a seller and useless for costing it. Four rooms of furniture you already own, stored ten minutes away, is a different cost from four rooms that empty your inventory for a quarter. What the money runs on is the carrying cost of the specific package you are committing and how long you expect to be without it, so quote in rooms if that is what the agent asks for, but build the number from the package.

Time on market decides your margin, not the staging price.

A staging quote covers an included term, but the furniture package keeps costing you storage, insurance, and wear for every month it sits in the house — and the market, not you, decides how long that is. This free calculator prices a job from that included term, then checks whether your extension fee even covers what an extra month costs you, and lets you plug in the real time on market once the listing sells. Common questions

Why does the calculator price the staging job at the included term instead of how long I expect the listing to take?

Because that is what a staging agreement actually promises: a price for an included term, with anything beyond it billed separately as an extension. Pricing the base fee from your expected time-on-market instead would double-count carrying cost for months that are supposed to be billed as an extension, not baked into the sticker price.

What happens if my extension fee is lower than my furniture carrying cost?

Every month the listing runs long then costs you more to keep that furniture package off the market than you charge the seller for it, so the fee meant to protect your margin instead erodes it — and the loss has no ceiling the longer the listing takes to sell. The calculator flags this directly and reports how many extension months would erase the job's entire built-in profit.

Why is the design consultation fee treated as pure profit with no added cost?

Because in this model the consultation is billed once regardless of term length and adds no furniture, storage, or crew cost of its own. If your business does incur a real added cost for it (a second visit, printed materials), fold that into the flat other-cost field.

Does anything about my job details get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing you type is saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-flat-per-room-rate.html.text:
← Home Staging Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-room rate

“$X a room, however long it takes” is not a price for a staging job — it is a price for install day, quietly stretched over however many months the furniture ends up sitting in the house.

What a flat per-room rate is

A flat per-room number is the fastest way to quote a vacant-listing job over the phone: count the rooms, multiply, and send the number. Sellers and agents like it because it is easy to compare across stagers, and it is the number a shopper holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it is usually set for install day — the crew hours, the mileage, the furniture going in — and then charged the same whether the listing sells in three weeks or sits on the market for a season, because a flat per-room rate has no line that changes with time.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter rooms staged, an included term, your furniture package's carrying cost per month, crew labor and mileage, equipment, overhead, and target margin. It prices the included term on its own cost, then checks whether the extension fee you charge past that term actually covers what the furniture keeps costing you to hold — storage, insurance, and wear — every month the listing does not sell. You get a price built on how long the furniture is actually deployed, not a flat number that assumes it away.

What a flat per-room rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same number whether the listing sells inside the included term or sits for months past it. Prices the included term on its own cost, then bills an explicit per-month extension fee for every month beyond it.
Has no check on whether the number it charges for extra time actually covers what the furniture costs to keep off the market. Compares the extension fee against the furniture's own carrying cost per month and flags it when the fee falls short.
Is set once from a room count and never revisited once the job is quoted. Lets you plug in the real time on market once the listing sells, to check the job's actual profit against the quote.
Gives you a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the profit margin at the included term and at the expected term, so a shopped price can be scored before you commit to it.

The same job, priced two ways

Using this calculator's own shipped defaults — 4 rooms staged, a 2-month included term, an expected 3-month time on market, $220/month furniture carrying cost, a $250/month extension fee, 6 crew hours at $30/hour, a 25-mile round trip, $40 in equipment, a $150 consult fee, 10% overhead, and a 30% target margin:

A flat rate of $200 a room for this 4-room job comes to $800. This calculator prices the same job's included term at $1,150.61, holding the target 30% margin on a $700.42 cost — the flat $800 quote still covers that cost, but only at a 12.45% margin, less than half the target. If the listing runs the expected extra month past the included term, this calculator's total price becomes $1,400.61 against a $920.42 total cost, still 34.28% margin — while the flat $800 quote, never adjusted for the extra month, now sits $120.42 below that cost. The flat rate does not just shrink the margin as the listing sits — past the included term, it goes into the red.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-room rate get a staging job wrong?

Because the number is set for install day -- crew hours, mileage, and the rooms furnished -- and has no line for how long the furniture then sits in the house. Using this calculator's own shipped defaults (4 rooms, a 2-month included term, $220/month furniture carrying cost, a $250/month extension fee), a $200-per-room flat quote comes to $800. That covers the calculator's own $700.42 included-term cost, but only at a 12.45% margin against the 30% this calculator targets -- and it does not move at all if the listing runs long.

What does a flat per-room rate usually leave out entirely?

A separate line for time on the market. The furniture package keeps costing storage, insurance, and wear for every month a listing does not sell, and a flat per-room number has no mechanism to bill for that once the included term runs out -- it was set once, on install day, and does not change if the home is still vacant a season later.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped defaults: a $200-per-room flat quote for 4 rooms is $800. This calculator prices the same job's included term at $1,150.61, holding a 30% margin on a $700.42 cost. If the listing runs the expected extra month past the included term, this calculator's total price becomes $1,400.61 against a $920.42 total cost -- still 34.28% margin -- while the flat $800 quote, never adjusted for the extra month, now sits $120.42 below that cost: a real loss, not just a thinner margin, once the furniture has been off the market long enough.

Is a flat per-room rate ever the right way to quote?

For a listing you are confident will sell inside the included term, a flat per-room number can land close, because that is the job it was probably set on. The risk is the listing that does not sell on schedule, because the rate does not know how long a home will sit, and by the time it is clear the term has run out the flat number has usually already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local furniture rental rates or how long homes sit in my market?

No. It has no data on your market's typical days on market, your supplier's furniture rental costs, or what other stagers in your area charge. It takes rooms staged, an included term, your furniture package's carrying cost per month, crew labor, mileage, equipment, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job and an extension fee check -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. HoneyBook

Two different shapes: HoneyBook is an account-based platform for running a creative or home-services business's client relationships end to end, including sending the contract and collecting the deposit once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this staging job cost, and does the extension fee actually cover what an extra month of carrying the furniture package really costs, before you send the number to the seller.

What each tool is for

HoneyBook is a client relationship and business management platform used by creative and home-services businesses — photographers, event planners, interior designers, and home stagers among them — for branded proposals, contracts with e-signatures, online invoicing and payments, scheduling, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. HoneyBook's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of CRM describe sending a proposal, collecting an e-signature and deposit, and invoicing the balance once a price already exists; none describe working out whether a vacant-listing staging price set for a two-month included term actually covers the furniture package's own monthly carrying cost, or whether an extension fee is set high enough to still turn a profit on a listing that runs long — which is what this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what HoneyBook does. It does not send a contract, collect an e-signature or deposit, or invoice a client. It takes rooms staged, the included term, furniture carrying cost, crew labor and mileage, equipment cost, a design consultation fee, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price for one vacant-listing job — plus a same-page check of whether the extension fee charged for every month beyond the included term actually clears the furniture package's own carrying cost, and a reconciliation once the listing's real time on market is known. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

vs-hutch.html.text:
← Home Staging Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Hutch

Two different shapes: Hutch is a paid, account-based platform for running a staging company's whole furniture inventory and project pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one job at a time — what should this vacant-listing staging price be, and does the extension fee actually cover what the furniture package costs to keep off the market, before you send the quote.

What each tool is for

Hutch (hutchstaging.com) is inventory and project management software built specifically for home staging businesses. It catalogues every piece of furniture and decor a company owns — with photos and item-level tags — tracks which pieces are deployed to which active listing, coordinates a team of stagers across several concurrent jobs, and keeps a client CRM, all on one paid account used on an ongoing basis. It is a real, purpose-built product for this trade, not a general project tool repurposed for staging. Outbound requests to hutchstaging.com are blocked from this session, so its current plan names and prices below are as reported by independent third-party software directories (StageCore's own published comparison and the aggregator WifiTalents), not confirmed directly against Hutch's own pricing page: those write-ups describe an entry-level plan in roughly the $100–$150 per month range, scaling with inventory size and team seats. Treat that figure as approximate and check hutchstaging.com for its current pricing.

This calculator does none of what Hutch does. It has no item catalogue, no photos, no team accounts, and no concept of which piece of furniture is in which house. It takes one job's numbers — the included term, the furniture package's total monthly carrying cost, crew labor, mileage, equipment cost, overhead, and target margin — and prices that single job, then checks whether the extension fee charged for running past the included term actually clears what the package costs to keep off the market for another listing. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Hutch?

They solve different problems, and a growing staging business will likely end up wanting both. Hutch is inventory and project management software built specifically for home staging companies: it catalogues every sofa, lamp, and accent chair a business owns (with photo storage and item-level tags), tracks which pieces are deployed to which active job, runs a client CRM, and coordinates a team across concurrent stages, on a paid monthly account. This calculator does none of that — it has no inventory catalogue, no per-item tracking, and no team accounts. It takes the numbers for one job (included term, furniture carrying cost, crew labor, mileage, equipment, and target margin) and prices that job, then flags when an extension fee is set below what the furniture package actually costs to keep off the market. A solo or small-crew stager who owns a single furniture package and wants a fast, free, no-signup answer to what to charge is in the right place here; a stager juggling dozens of pieces across several simultaneous jobs, who needs to know which items are where, is better served by Hutch or a comparable inventory platform.

Does this calculator track my furniture inventory the way Hutch does?

No. This calculator has no item catalogue, no photos, no tags, and no concept of "which pieces are in which house." You enter one number — your furniture package's total carrying cost per month — and the calculator uses it to price the job and check the extension fee. If you need to know which lamp is at which listing, or manage a multi-piece inventory across a team, that is what a dedicated platform like Hutch is for.
